extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, law students, and litigators studying patent validity and remedies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on defenses to patent validity (public use, sale, abandonment, surreptitious patents, priority) and on equitable remedies (injunction practice and parties entitled). Intended to inform litigation strategy and statutory interpretation under 19th-century Acts and case law precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use or sale with consent or allowance (statutory defence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defence that the invention was in 'public use or exercise of it, by a single instance of a transaction' with the 'consent or allowance of the patentee' prior to application (Act/section language).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patentee has put the invention into public use or sold it (i.e., as an article of commerce) to any one of the public who might buy, the invention may not be new at the date of the patent. A single sale to any purchaser might, under some circumstances, be deemed the commencement of a practice and a public use sufficient to defeat a patent. The courts analyze whether the transaction was effectively a public use (for profit/commerce) rather than a private transaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Private or confidential construction/use does not equal public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the inventor had machines constructed under secrecy and an injunction of secrecy, and disclosure was to a person connected with the inventor and intending to share the patent, such disclosure is 'private and confidential' and not a public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use or construction done under express secrecy or on the inventor's private premises, or disclosed only to persons in privity with the inventor (e.g., prospective co-inventor or licensee), will not generally be treated as public use. Treat as equivalent to the inventor having made the machines in his private workshop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale for profit or as article of commerce defeats novelty
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee himself had constructed machines for sale 'as an article of commerce, for gain to himself,' and publicly sold them to any buyer, the invention would not be new at the date of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts emphasize the risk that allowing secret commercial sales would permit the inventor to extend practical monopoly beyond statutory term. Even sales fit only for foreign markets or single sales could be held to commence public practice depending on circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use arising from breach of confidence (piratical user) does not constitute consent/allowance
rubrics_metrics.description: When the invention has come into public use through a breach of confidence by a person to whom knowledge was imparted confidentially, such use is not 'with the consent or allowance' of the patentee; the presumption of consent arises only if the patentee remains silent after it becomes public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a confidentially-informed party piratically makes the invention public, the inventor may still obtain a valid patent provided he takes immediate steps (e.g., giving notice of his exclusive right). The statute and case law treat unauthorized disclosure differently from permissive public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited permission for experimental or accommodation purposes is not public use
rubrics_metrics.description: If the patentee allows others a limited use, not for his own profit but for their accommodation (consistent with clear intention to retain exclusivity and with the invention remaining under his control), that use will not be treated as public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts apply tests (e.g., Morgan v. Seaward) to assess whether permitted use exceeded experimental/limited object or manifested an intention to abandon exclusivity. Acts consistent with neighborly kindness or limited convenience, kept within the patentee's control, typically do not defeat a patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mere delay to apply for patent (without public use) does not forfeit rights
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere delay by the inventor to take out a patent, unaccompanied by public use or sale with consent/allowance before his application, will have no effect on the validity of the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delay is only probative insofar as it tends to show acquiescence in public use or that the inventor's acts went beyond permitted experimental use. The absence of sale/use with consent means delay alone doesn't constitute abandonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of 1839 §7 — prior purchaser/constructor protection and 2-year limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory provision: every person or corporation who purchased or constructed a newly-invented machine, manufacture, or composition of matter prior to the inventor's application 'shall be held to possess the right to use, and vend to others to be used, the specific machine... without liability' and 'no patent shall be held to be invalid by reason of such purchase, sale, or use... except on proof of abandonment of such invention to the public; or that such purchase, sale, or prior use, has been for more than two years prior to such application.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This statute protects prior purchasers/users of the specific thing made before application, allowing their continued use/sale without liability, and preserves the patentee's patent except when abandonment to the public is shown or when the prior use/sale extended over more than two years before application. The act does not make prior sale/use per se fatal to patent validity; context matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment to the public must be proved by more than the particular prior act alone
rubrics_metrics.description: A particular purchase, sale, or prior use before application does not of itself invalidate a patent unless it 'amount[s] to an abandonment to the public' or is shown by additional facts/deeds outside the specific act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts require that the individual act be connected with circumstances showing broader abandonment, or that other disconnected acts/omissions by the patentee demonstrate an intention to abandon. The obvious construction is that isolated prior sales/uses are insufficient unless linked to abandonment or exceed the two-year period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act of 1839 construed to embrace all patentable subject-matter ('invention patented')
rubrics_metrics.description: Although the statute uses the phrase 'newly-invented machine, manufacture, or composition of matter,' the U.S. Supreme Court construed these terms to mean 'the invention patented,' whatever it may be; thus the provision applies to processes and methods as well as machines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The court interpreted 'specific machine' to refer to 'the thing as originally invented' so the statute's protection and limitations extend to the subject-matter of a valid patent (including processes/methods), avoiding a hyper-literal construction that would defeat the act's objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence that patentee surreptitiously or unjustly obtained patent (priority by another)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statutory defence: that the patentee had 'surreptitiously or unjustly obtained the patent for that which was in fact invented or discovered by another, who was using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting the same.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended to cover patents obtained by fraud or where two independent inventors exist and the later applicant secures a patent first. If the prior inventor was using reasonable diligence to adapt/perfect the invention, that prior activity can bar the later patent holder. Courts analyze both fraud/surreptitious procurement and competing-first-inventor scenarios.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption of notice from prior patent office records
rubrics_metrics.description: When the real inventor files a description at the patent office or obtains a patent, that filing gives notice to subsequent applicants; a jury may infer piracy by the existence of the former record because subsequent patentees are presumed to have knowledge of public records.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Filing a specification/record creates a presumption that later applicants are or should be aware of the prior record (constructive notice). Courts treat this as evidence from which a jury can infer that a subsequent patentee pirated the invention if other facts support the inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority dispute rule: 'reasonable diligence' and reduction to practice
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor who first actually perfects and adapts an invention is ordinarily entitled to a patent; but the clause qualifies that, giving priority to the first inventor if he was 'using reasonable diligence in adapting and perfecting the same.' Mere speculative or unperfected theories are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An imperfect, theoretical, or incomplete invention not reduced to practice is not patentable; in a race between independent inventors, the one who first reduces to a fixed, practical form usually has priority, except when an earlier inventor can show reasonable diligence in adapting/perfecting the invention — in which case priority may lie with the earlier inventor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign/alien patentee sales requirement (18-month rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provision that a patentee who was an alien at the time the patent was granted 'had failed and neglected for the space of eighteen months from the date of the patent, to put and continue on sale to the public, on reasonable terms, the invention or discovery' — aimed to prevent foreign inventors from obtaining patents and withholding use for an unreasonable time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This special provision imposes a time-based duty on alien patentees to make the invention available on reasonable terms, or face the statutory consequence; purpose is to protect domestic public access when foreign patentees otherwise withhold use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equitable jurisdiction and grounds for injunctions in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity provides a preventive remedy (injunction) where legal damages would be inadequate; grounds include prevention of irreparable mischief, suppression of multiplicity of suits and vexatious litigation, and more complete discovery of the extent of injury.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An injunction complements legal remedies; courts of equity act where prevention of future harm is indispensable or where discovery/accounting by the infringer is necessary. This is the statutory and doctrinal basis for seeking injunctions in patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretion of equity courts in granting injunctions and interlocutory options
rubrics_metrics.description: The statute vests discretion to grant injunctions 'according to the course and principles of courts of equity' and 'on such terms and conditions as the said courts may deem reasonable.' Courts may (interlocutorily) grant injunctions simpliciter, grant them while directing the plaintiff to establish title at law, suspend grant pending legal investigation (defendant keeping accounts), or dismiss/retain the bill at hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The discretion is guided by established equitable principles: the court chooses the remedy that does justice between the parties. At hearing the court may sometimes grant final injunctions without a law trial if satisfied; otherwise it may retain the bill for the plaintiff to prove title at law or impose conditions. Factors include conduct of parties, validity questions, and evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may sue in equity for infringement; assignee and recording rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties entitled to equitable relief are the persons 'interested in the patent' — patentees, assignees, or grantees of exclusive rights. If an assignee has the whole interest he may sue alone; if less than whole interest he must join the patentee. An unrecorded assignment does not substitute the assignee to maintain suits without joining the patentee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equitable practice follows statutory rules about who holds the legal title to enforce patent rights. Where assignments are not recorded, the assignee may lack standing to sue alone; where only a local/exclusive right is granted (grantee for a district), that grantee may bring actions at law in its own district (distinction noted between law and equity). Courts will apply the same rules in equity as in law regarding necessary parties and recorded assignments.
